Friday-Saturday: The next upper-level trough approaches today and 
limps inland tonight into Saturday. The slow movement is due to
an appreciable amount of meridional stretching while also 
taking on a slight negative tilt. Friday will deliver one more 
dry day before a band of light rain slowly tracks west to east 
Friday night into Saturday. Higher range of the rainfall totals 
will be near 0.25 inches for locations near the Cascade Crest 
and around the Camas Prairie. Between these areas, rainfall 
amounts will range anywhere from a trace to less than 0.15 
inches. We are observing a heavy influx in high clouds right now
and this is limiting fog development so far despite a very 
moist boundary layer. Motorists will encounter patchy areas of 
dense fog Friday morning but confidence is low that conditions 
will warrant the extent of dense fog that we have observed over 
the last few mornings. Breezy east to southeast winds across the
Camas Prairie, L-C Valley, and Palouse will keep these areas 
fog and low cloud free. 

Winds will largely be out of the east and southeast across the 
Inland NW will breezy conditions across the ridgetops and 
across the lowland expanding from the Palouse to the Waterville 
Plateau. Local wind gusts of 20-30 mph will be common with gusts
closer to 35 mph along higher ridgelines. The easterly flow 
will keep temperatures cooler across the East Slopes of the 
Cascades and mild from Lewiston to Grand Coulee topping out in 
the upper 50s to lower 60s. Winds will shift back to the 
west/southwest Friday night into Saturday with the arrival of 
the cold front. The westerly push will be weak but still capable
of breezes of 10-20 mph. Areas of low stratus will be likely 
with the rain with Friday night into Saturday morning with 
patchy fog Temperatures will cool back into the 50s for Saturday
with increased odds for areas of dense fog redeveloping 
Saturday night. 

Sunday-Thursday: Storm systems will continue to move across the
Eastern Pacific and into the Pac NW. However, the general trend
will be for these systems will be to weaken while coming 
onshore with the strongest dynamics coming in south of the 
Inland NW. So while there is moderate confidence for additional 
rounds of precipitation, at this time there are no signals for 
any real impactful storm systems. The next cold front and period
of precipitation will arrive Sunday. This system will have a 
bit more jet dynamics to work with versus Friday night's front 
and less dry air to overcome equating to more areas receiving 
between a 0.10 and 0.40 inches of rain and upwards of 0.50 for 
the Cascade Crest. Cooler air will arrive with this system 
leading to increasing chances for light snow on Sherman and 
Washington Passes for Sunday. There is lower confidence for snow
impacts at Stevens Sunday with snow levels not falling close to
pass level until Sunday night as precipitation is winding down.
Lookout Pass will remain on the warm side of the front through 
Sunday with no concerns for snow. Sunday's trough will also 
undergo meridional stretching slowing down the cold front 
passage through Idaho through the day on Monday and in general, 
this will not create a lot of wind across the region as we cool 
down the air mass to more typical November standards. Something 
to monitor will be a transition from rain to snow for Lookout 
Pass and over the higher benches of the Camas Prairie Monday 
night into Tuesday morning with indication of 850mb temperatures
dipping near 0 to -0.5C. Tuesday looks to be a transition day 
with the Sunday-Monday front shifting east and another deep low 
wobbling toward the coast. The track of this system comes with 
50% of the ensembles favoring a track south of the Inland NW 
through N CA and Oregon while 50% are further north across WA-
OR. With a cooler air mass in place, this will need to be 
monitored closely for more impactful snow on the mountain passes
and mix of rain and wet snow for some lowlands, especially 
around the Camas Prairie, Palouse, and Blue Mountains. 

Friday-weekend: There is good agreement (80-90%) that high 
pressure will return to the Northwest bringing another period of
light winds and dry conditions. There is a strong likelihood 
that this will promote another period of expansive fog and low 
clouds following in the wake of precipitation events this week. 
This will likely result in cooler, near normal temperatures 
given the poor mixing. /sb
